questions.hint: Match the requested aggregation and units, rather than choosing by the metric name alone.

questions.concept: Why Accuracy Fails on Imbalanced Data
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the majority-class accuracy baseline and its failure to detect positives.
questions.question: A validation set is \(99\%\) negative and \(1\%\) positive. Why is an always-negative classifier inadequate if detecting positive cases matters?

options.label: A
options.text: It achieves \(99\%\) accuracy but detects none of the actual positive cases.

options.label: B
options.text: It achieves \(1\%\) accuracy because only the minority-class fraction counts as correct.

options.label: C
options.text: It achieves \(99\%\) positive-class recall because most observations are negative.

questions.explanation: All actual negatives are correctly predicted, giving \(99\%\) accuracy. Every actual positive is missed, so recall is \(0\). Accuracy is mathematically valid, but used alone it can hide this failure on an operationally important minority class.
questions.hint: Count what happens separately to examples of each actual class.

questions.concept: Recall Optimization Under a False-Positive Constraint
questions.learningObjective: Select the highest-recall screening threshold that satisfies a false-positive constraint.
questions.question: In a hypothetical screening validation set, there are \(100\) actual positive cases. A high threshold gives \(70\) true positives and \(5\) false positives; a medium threshold gives \(85\) and \(10\); a low threshold gives \(90\) and \(20\). You require at most \(10\) false positives and then maximize recall. Which threshold should be chosen?

options.label: A
options.text: The low threshold.

options.label: B
options.text: The high threshold.

options.label: C
options.text: The medium threshold.

questions.explanation: The low threshold violates the false-positive limit because \(20>10\). The high and medium thresholds satisfy it; their recalls are \(\frac{70}{100}=70\%\) and \(\frac{85}{100}=85\%\). The medium threshold therefore has the highest recall among feasible choices. Threshold selection uses validation data, with final test evaluation kept separate.
questions.hint: Check feasibility first, then compare the relevant detection proportions among the feasible choices.

questions.learningObjective: Define generalization in terms of performance on fresh relevant examples.
questions.question: What is meant by 'generalization' in Machine Learning?

options.label: A
options.text: The ability to perform well on fresh examples from the relevant target population.

options.label: B
options.text: The ability to reproduce every training target without any error.

options.label: C
options.text: The act of rescaling all numerical input features into a common range.

questions.explanation: Generalization concerns performance beyond the fitted sample on examples relevant to the intended task. Perfect training fit alone does not establish this. A representative independent evaluation helps assess it, while population shifts can change the generalization requirement.
questions.hint: Think about the prediction objective after fitting is complete.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize systematic error of the average fitted predictor as bias.
questions.question: A straight-line regression family is fitted to many random training samples from a known curved relationship. Even the average of its fitted predictions systematically misses the curvature. Which effect is illustrated?

options.label: A
options.text: Sampling variance: differences among individual fitted predictors around their average.

options.label: B
options.text: Approximation bias: systematic deviation of the average predictor from the true relationship.

options.label: C
options.text: Observation noise: random target changes unrelated to the input relationship.

questions.explanation: The persistent mismatch of the average fitted predictor with the true relationship is bias. A straight-line family may be unable to represent curvature even with plentiful data. Variance concerns differences between fitted predictors; observation noise concerns unpredictable target variation, not this systematic representation error.
questions.hint: Separate the average fitted predictor from the variation among individual fitted predictors.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize variability across fitted training samples as prediction variance.
questions.question: Flexible regression models fitted on different same-sized random samples from one population predict very different values at the same fixed input. Their average prediction is close to the known true response. Which effect is primarily illustrated?

options.label: A
options.text: High approximation bias, because the average prediction misses the true response.

options.label: B
options.text: A change in the deployment population, because the training examples were resampled.

options.label: C
options.text: High prediction variance, because the fitted result is sensitive to the training sample.

questions.explanation: The spread of fitted predictions at a fixed input across random training samples measures variance. A close average prediction suggests low bias at that input, but does not eliminate the spread. Resampling from the same population does not itself establish deployment distribution shift.
questions.hint: Keep systematic average error distinct from instability between separately fitted models.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish sparsity encouraged by L1 from the usual shrinkage behavior of L2.
questions.question: For standard penalized linear regression with positive regularization strength, which statement describes a typical difference between L1 (Lasso) and L2 (Ridge) penalties?

options.label: A
options.text: L2 commonly performs sparse feature selection, while L1 keeps every coefficient nonzero.

options.label: B
options.text: L1 can set some coefficients exactly to zero; L2 generally shrinks coefficients without promoting sparsity.

options.label: C
options.text: L1 is used only for neural networks, while L2 is used only for linear regression.

questions.explanation: L1 uses \(\lambda\sum_j|w_j|\), which can produce sparse solutions. L2 uses \(\lambda\sum_j w_j^2\), which generally shrinks coefficients without promoting exact zeros. A Ridge coefficient can still be zero in particular data configurations; Lasso does not guarantee selecting exactly the truly relevant features.
questions.hint: Compare the geometry of an absolute-value penalty with a smooth squared penalty near zero.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a validation experiment when excessive regularization is the supported cause of underfitting.
questions.question: A converged model misses learnable patterns in both training and validation data. Controlled experiments identify excessively strong regularization as the limiting factor. Which next experiment addresses that cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the regularization strength while keeping the model family unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Try weaker regularization and compare candidates using training-only cross-validation.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the regularization strength and fit only to a smaller random subset of the same data.

questions.explanation: Weaker regularization permits a closer fit when the current penalty is suppressing learnable structure. Select its strength using validation or cross-validation and monitor overfitting. Low performance without the stated controlled evidence would not uniquely identify excessive regularization as the cause.
questions.hint: Use the stated cause to decide which restriction should be varied.

questions.learningObjective: Explain data quality as a potential limit on prediction without an absolute failure claim.
questions.question: Which statement accurately reflects 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' in predictive modeling?

options.label: A
options.text: A sufficiently flexible model makes incorrect feature values harmless in every dataset.

options.label: B
options.text: Incorrect, noisy, or uninformative inputs can limit predictive performance even with a powerful model.

options.label: C
options.text: A high validation score proves that all recorded input features are accurate and relevant.

questions.explanation: Prediction quality can be constrained by incorrect values, measurement noise, missing signal, or unreliable targets. A powerful model does not remove the need for data checks. Some algorithms can ignore irrelevant features or tolerate noise, so poor inputs do not guarantee failure in every dataset.
questions.hint: Separate useful signal from model capacity and consider whether inputs faithfully represent the task.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how domain knowledge supports useful, available, and leakage-safe feature construction.
questions.question: How can domain knowledge improve feature engineering for prediction?

options.label: A
options.text: It proves that every strongly correlated feature has a causal effect on the target.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes validation unnecessary once a plausible feature has been proposed.

options.label: C
options.text: It helps propose meaningful predictive features and check availability, leakage, and implausible transformations.

questions.explanation: Domain knowledge can reveal useful representations and expose impossible values or features recorded only after the target event. A useful predictive association need not be causal. Proposed features still require valid evaluation, and causal claims require evidence beyond predictive correlation.
questions.hint: Consider whether a promising recorded field would be available when the prediction must be made.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an optimizer-learned weight from a validation-selected training setting in a concrete run.
questions.question: In a neural-network run, an optimizer changes a weight using loss gradients. Separately, a search picks a learning rate by comparing validation scores. Which is a learned model parameter?

options.label: A
options.text: The weight changed by the optimizer.

options.label: B
options.text: The learning rate picked by the validation search.

options.label: C
options.text: The hidden-layer count fixed for the candidate architecture.

questions.explanation: The weight is part of the fitted prediction function and is updated through the fitting objective. The learning rate and layer count configure training or architecture in this run. Automated, data-informed selection of a learning rate does not turn it into a fitted weight parameter in the described setup.
questions.hint: Ask which operation selected each value, rather than whether a person typed it.

questions.concept: Counting Updates with a Partial Batch
questions.learningObjective: Count mini-batch updates for an epoch that retains a final partial batch.
questions.question: A conventional training loop visits \(10{,}050\) examples once per epoch with batch size \(1{,}000\). It keeps the final partial batch and performs one optimizer update per batch, with no gradient accumulation. How many updates occur in one epoch?
questions.explanation: Ten full batches process \(10{,}000\) examples, leaving \(50\) in one partial batch. Thus the update count is \(\left\lceil\frac{10{,}050}{1{,}000}\right\rceil=11\). Dropping the partial batch or accumulating gradients would change the result, so both conventions are specified.
questions.hint: Account for any examples left after all full batches have been processed.

questions.learningObjective: Describe memory and gradient-noise trade-offs when reducing batch size.
questions.question: For the same neural network, what is a typical trade-off when using smaller mini-batches rather than the full dataset per update?

options.label: A
options.text: Less batch-dependent memory and a guarantee of higher final prediction accuracy.

options.label: B
options.text: Less batch-dependent activation memory but generally noisier gradient estimates per update.

options.label: C
options.text: Less batch-dependent memory and a guarantee of faster end-to-end convergence.

questions.explanation: Smaller batches usually need less memory for examples and activations and yield noisier gradient estimates under ordinary sampling. With one update per batch, they also give more updates per epoch. Total speed and convergence depend on hardware utilization, throughput, optimization settings, and data; accuracy gains or escape from minima are not guaranteed.
questions.hint: Compare what must be stored for one update and how many observations determine its gradient.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the input-vector size for a simple dense network with one value per tabular feature.
questions.question: A simple fully connected network receives a tabular vector with \(N\) scalar features, with no embedding or other representation expansion. How many input values does each example supply?
questions.explanation: The supplied input vector has dimension \(N\), one scalar value per feature in this setup. A bias is a model term rather than an extra required data feature. Image tensors, sequences, embeddings, and other architectures have different input structures, so this is not a universal rule about all neural networks.
questions.hint: Write down the shape of one preprocessed example before considering hidden-layer width.

questions.learningObjective: Describe hidden layers as learned intermediate transformations in a feed-forward model.
questions.question: What is a typical role of hidden layers with nonlinear activations in a feed-forward neural network?

options.label: A
options.text: They directly define one final probability output for each target class.

options.label: B
options.text: They store the full training dataset as a required lookup table.

options.label: C
options.text: They learn intermediate transformations that can support complex input-output relationships.

questions.explanation: Hidden layers transform input representations through learned weights and nonlinearities. These intermediate representations can support complex relationships used by later layers. They are not guaranteed to become increasingly interpretable or abstract with depth, and they need not store the training examples explicitly.
questions.hint: Distinguish intermediate computation from the final target representation.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the output-logit count for standard single-label softmax classification.
questions.question: A network predicts exactly one of \(10\) digit classes using a standard softmax output with one logit per class. How many output logits are needed?
questions.explanation: The stated representation requires \(10\) logits, one for each class, which softmax converts to \(10\) probabilities summing to \(1\). The hidden-layer width and number of training examples do not determine this output count. Other parameterizations would need their own explicit convention.
questions.hint: Determine how many distinct class scores the specified output representation must produce.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a bias term as an additive pre-activation intercept in a dense neuron.
questions.question: In a typical dense neuron that includes a bias term, what role does that bias serve?

options.label: A
options.text: It multiplies each input by a learned scale before all inputs are summed.

options.label: B
options.text: It adds an input-independent intercept to the weighted sum before activation.

options.label: C
options.text: It sets the step size used by the optimizer to update the weights.

questions.explanation: With a bias, the pre-activation is \(z=\sum_j w_jx_j+b\). The additive term \(b\) allows a nonzero intercept even when all inputs are zero. This mathematical bias is distinct from social bias or approximation bias; some layers disable the bias term, so it is not present in every neuron.
questions.hint: Compare changing an input multiplier with changing a constant in the fitted expression.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the chain rule to a scalar weight gradient of a squared-error loss.
questions.question: A scalar linear neuron has \(\hat{y}=wx\) and loss \(L=\frac{1}{2}(\hat{y}-y)^2\). With \(x=2\), \(w=3\), and \(y=4\), what is \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\)?
questions.explanation: Use the chain rule: \[\begin{aligned}\hat{y}&=3\cdot 2=6\\\frac{\partial L}{\partial\hat{y}}&=\hat{y}-y=2\\\frac{\partial\hat{y}}{\partial w}&=x=2\\\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}&=2\cdot 2=4\end{aligned}\] The derivative is not just the residual: the input factor must be included. Backpropagation applies this principle efficiently through larger computation graphs.
questions.hint: Trace how changing the weight changes the prediction and then the loss; include both derivatives.
